name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Wednesday 9 November 1983

clue.text: Record a little power rise in this vehicle

indicators.note: in a down clue, to rise is to go upward, so the string reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: to note something is to record it
taken as written
hp, horsepower, is a unit of power, and 'little' asks for the abbreviation

explanation.surface: A logbook entry noting a small power increase in some vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: A phaeton is a light, open, four-wheeled carriage, and later an open touring car: a vehicle either way.

clue.text: Writes of hundreds brought up by a river quarter

indicators.note: to be brought up by someone is to be raised in their care, so one piece sits enclosed within the other

blocks.note: south, one of the four quarters of the compass
C is the Roman hundred; more than one gives CS
the Ribble is a river in northern England

explanation.surface: A river quarter's chronicles, reaching back hundreds of years.
explanation.walkthrough: The parse is loose: CS takes the Ribble inside it and S, a compass quarter, goes in front. The Ribble flows through Lancashire to the Irish Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: To scribble is to write hastily or carelessly, so scribbles is a loose synonym for writes.

clue.text: March off through pass?

blocks.note: first meaning: to march off in single file, as troops do
second meaning: a narrow gorge or pass through mountains

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures soldiers marching out through a pass; the two ends are separate meanings, and a defile is just where troops must go in file.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb the word means to file past in a line; as a noun it is a narrow valley or passage.

clue.text: Recoil from cat, perhaps?

blocks.note: first meaning: a sudden recoil or violent reaction
second meaning, read literally: a stroke across the back from the cat-o'-nine-tails, a whip

explanation.walkthrough: The cat here is the cat-o'-nine-tails, a many-tailed whip, and 'perhaps' warns that this second reading is playful: what the cat gives is a lash on the back.
explanation.definitionFit: A backlash is a sharp recoil, originally the jarring rebound of machinery, and now any strong adverse reaction.

clue.text: Is the last sort of bushranger? Tripe!

indicators.note: a sort of something is a variant of it, so the letters that follow are rearranged

blocks.note: ten letters, taken as written
five more letters, taken as written

explanation.surface: A scoffing question about whether this is the last of the bushrangers, dismissed as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tripe!' reads as an exclamation of scorn, but it is part of the letters to mix. Bushrangers were outlaws of the Australian bush, such as Ned Kelly.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring up the rear is an idiom for coming last in a procession or race.

clue.text: Legislature study note about bodyguard

blocks.note: to con is an old word for to study or learn
G is a musical note
re means about or concerning
the SS began as Hitler's personal bodyguard unit

explanation.surface: Lawmakers examine a memo about someone's personal security.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is only a piece here, not a container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Congress is the national legislative body of the United States and some other republics.

clue.text: House with ground?

blocks.note: first meaning: the House of ..., upper chamber of the UK Parliament
second meaning: ..., the London cricket ground

explanation.walkthrough: A house with grounds sounds like an estate; the two words are a parliamentary chamber and a sports ground sharing a name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lords is shorthand for the upper House of Parliament, and Lord's is the famous cricket ground in St John's Wood, London.

clue.text: Tennis ace appears pleasant - an amiable type

indicators.note: something that appears comes into sight, so the name shows itself inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word through the second into the start of the third
surface padding that rounds off the phrase 'an amiable type'

explanation.surface: A tennis star comes across as a nice, friendly sort.
explanation.definitionFit: Manuel Santana was a Spanish tennis champion who won Wimbledon in 1966, so he is a tennis ace.

clue.text: Chewing-gum is fashionable - the foreign sort

blocks.note: chic means stylish or fashionable
le is the French word for 'the'

explanation.surface: A complaint that a trendy brand of chewing-gum is imported.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The foreign sort' asks for a foreign-language 'the'; French LE is the usual choice.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicle is the natural latex from the sapodilla tree that was the original base of chewing-gum, so it stands for the gum itself.

clue.text: Not knowing Signor Antonio's part?

indicators.note: a part of something is a piece of it, so the letters sit inside the neighbouring words

blocks.note: the letters run across the two names, skipping the opening S

explanation.surface: Someone unaware of the role an Italian gentleman named Antonio plays, as if casting a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part' suggests a theatrical role for Signor Antonio, as in The Merchant of Venice; it really means a portion of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignorant means lacking knowledge or unaware, which is exactly what 'not knowing' describes.

clue.text: Mockery returns - no one's annoyed

indicators.note: something that returns comes back the way it went, so the following words are read from right to left

blocks.note: taken as written
one is I, and the 's stands for 'is'
ired means angered or annoyed

explanation.surface: A reaction to ridicule: when the mockery comes back, nobody minds.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'no one's annoyed' look like a comment; it is the wordplay, read backwards in full.
explanation.definitionFit: Derision is scornful ridicule, a close synonym of mockery.

clue.text: Scamp reveals the painter's state

blocks.note: RA, a Royal Academician, is the crossword painter; add the 's
Cal is a short form of California, a US state

explanation.surface: A mischievous child gives away what condition an artist is in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like 'condition' in the surface, but it is a US state.
explanation.definitionFit: A scamp and a rascal are both a mischievous, roguish person, usually said fondly of a child.

clue.text: Drinks for the workers at last!

blocks.note: first meaning: iced drinks of wine or sherry with fruit and sugar
second meaning: shoemakers, who work at a last, the foot-shaped block a shoe is built on

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is drinks for workers when the shift finally ends; 'at last' is really the shoemaker's last.
explanation.definitionFit: A cobbler is both a long iced drink and a mender of shoes, so the plural covers drinks and the workers.

clue.text: Misanthropic soul, Cain? Could be

indicators.note: the question 'could be?' suggests these words could become something else when their letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the eight letters of the two words, ignoring the comma

explanation.surface: Wondering whether Cain, the Bible's first murderer, was a people-hating soul.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unsocial avoids the company of others, which is the core of misanthropy, a dislike of people.

clue.text: Promise £100 for various anthologists

indicators.note: various suggests the letters taken in different arrangements, so they are shuffled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the pound sign is L, from Latin libra, and 100 is Roman C

explanation.surface: An offer of a hundred pounds to assorted editors of collections.
explanation.walkthrough: '£100' must be split into its symbols: the pound sign gives L and the number gives C.
explanation.definitionFit: An anthologist gathers pieces by others into a single book, which is the work of a compiler.

clue.text: Car driver carries points by producing old pistol

indicators.note: whatever carries something holds it within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: petrol is the fuel that drives a car
two compass points, north and east

explanation.surface: A motorist carrying a weapon is charged and loses points on their licence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Car driver' wants to be a motorist, but it is what drives a car: its fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: A petronel was a large horse pistol or carbine of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

clue.text: Chance of success in view?

blocks.note: first meaning: a likelihood of future success
second meaning: an extensive scene or outlook

explanation.walkthrough: 'In view' reads as a phrase meaning 'foreseeable', but 'in' only joins the two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A prospect is both an expectation of something good to come and a wide landscape seen from a vantage point.

clue.text: Flashy fliers and swimmers

blocks.note: the Royal Air Force, Britain's military fliers
fish are swimmers

explanation.surface: Birds and fish with showy, brilliant colouring.
explanation.walkthrough: The RAF is Britain's air force; 'fliers' sounds like birds in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Raffish means flashy in a slightly disreputable, rakish way.

clue.text: A sort of tropic fruit

indicators.note: a sort of something is a version of it, so the word that follows is rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
six letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Describing a kind of tropical fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A sort of tropic fruit' wants to be mango or papaya; the fruit is not tropical at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The apricot is a small orange stone fruit related to the plum and peach.

clue.text: Dance in cape and hose, perhaps

blocks.note: Cape Horn, the southern tip of South America, is the famous cape
a hose is a flexible pipe; 'perhaps' flags the example

explanation.surface: Someone dancing in a cloak and stockings, like an Elizabethan courtier.
explanation.walkthrough: Cape and hose look like period costume, but they are a headland and a tube.
explanation.definitionFit: The hornpipe is a lively solo dance traditionally associated with sailors.

clue.text: Strong gold mount on sculpture

indicators.note: to mount is to climb, and in a down clue climbing means the letters read upward

blocks.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
a bust is a sculpture of head and shoulders

explanation.surface: A sturdy gold setting for a statue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' reads as a setting or base in the surface, but it is a verb for climbing; 'on' puts the gold above the sculpture.
explanation.definitionFit: Robust means sturdy and powerful, a direct synonym of strong.

clue.text: Something to do with love of business?

blocks.note: first meaning: a romantic liaison
second meaning: a matter or concern, as in 'that is my business'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Love of business' reads as a fondness for commerce; split it, and 'of' merely joins two meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: An affair is a romantic liaison and also a matter or piece of business, as in one's financial affairs.

clue.text: French city has real' difficulty over Sunday opening

indicators.note: letters in difficulty are in trouble and thrown out of order, so they are rearranged
an opening is a beginning, so only the first letter of the word is taken

blocks.note: four letters to be rearranged
the first letter of the day

explanation.surface: A French city where something goes badly wrong as Sunday begins.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'over' places the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Arles is a city in Provence in southern France, known for its Roman ruins and for Van Gogh.

clue.text: Writer reversed Spanish assent to drink bar

indicators.note: 'reversed' says the whole string that follows is to be read from its far end back to the start

blocks.note: si is Spanish for yes
ale is a drink, beer
taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer turns down a Spanish invitation to go drinking in a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reversed' looks like the writer's action in the surface; it applies to all three pieces after it.
explanation.definitionFit: François Rabelais was a French Renaissance author, best known for Gargantua and Pantagruel.

clue.text: Fault about poor Noel presented with excessive force

indicators.note: something in poor shape is out of order, so the name's letters are mixed up
about means around, so the fault wraps itself round the other piece

blocks.note: a vice is a moral fault or failing
the name supplies four letters to be mixed

explanation.surface: A complaint about poor Noel, whose faults were laid bare far too forcefully.
explanation.definitionFit: Violence is the use of physical force, especially force that is excessive or unlawful.

clue.text: Address familiar to people in the services

definitions.text: Address familiar to people in the services

blocks.clueFragment: Address familiar to people in the services
blocks.note: surface reading: a forces mailing address, or a way of speaking known to soldiers and sailors

blocks.clueFragment: Address familiar to people in the services
blocks.note: setter's reading: a speech heard by congregations attending church services

explanation.walkthrough: 'The services' points to the armed forces; it means church services, and 'address' is a speech, not a location.
explanation.definitionFit: A sermon is a talk on a religious theme delivered by a preacher during worship.

clue.text: Artist using breathing space to make notes

definitions.text: using breathing space to make notes

blocks.note: first meaning: James McNeill ..., the American painter of '... Mother'

blocks.clueFragment: using breathing space to make notes
blocks.note: second meaning: someone producing musical notes by blowing air through pursed lips

explanation.walkthrough: 'Make notes' suggests jotting things down; here the notes are musical, made with the breath.
explanation.definitionFit: The painter's surname is also the everyday word for a person who whistles a tune.
